idiom_name: unexported fields + NewX constructor + value receivers with WithX copy-on-write
implementation_notes: Go has no immutability declaration, so the idiom is a package discipline: keep the fields unexported so only the defining package can touch them, expose a constructor that validates and returns a value, and write methods on value receivers that return a new value (WithX) instead of mutating the receiver. Assigning the struct copies it, so small values are naturally independent - but the copy is shallow: slices, maps and pointer fields still alias, and they must be cloned on the way in and out. Nothing stops code in the same package, and nothing stops the zero value, so the ownership rule has to be documented at the trust boundary.
pitfalls: A struct copy copies the slice or map header, not the backing array: a getter that returns the internal slice, or a wither that appends without slices.Clone, mutates what every other holder sees.
Unexported fields do not protect against code in the same package, and the zero value (var p Point) bypasses the constructor, so invariants must be re-checked at boundaries such as JSON decoding.
A constructor returning *T reintroduces sharing: if callers receive a pointer and the type has any mutating method, the value is mutable again - return T for values and avoid pointer receivers.
